title: paper-harvest-playground-milestone-notes
content:
Purpose: quick personal harvest from a short sprint (3 days) of paper skim + workshop talks. Save here so I can turn into a small runbook for an initial probing experiment on Redwood runtime. Not polished — very much a sandbox scratchpad.

High-level theme I care about: long-context economics for production inference. Which levers give the largest SLO/cost wins when we have to serve conversational long-history workloads? Papers below + rough ideas.

Paper 1 — "Sparse Prefix KV for Long-Range Context" (skim notes)
- Core idea: instead of caching all prefix KV per token, keep a sparse selection of KV entries selected by (1) recency, (2) salience score (learned or heuristic), (3) coarse clustering.
- Why it matters: reduces memory pressure and improves cache hit utility for longer windows.
- Observations for us: maps well to Redwood's smart routing + caching layer — could implement as an eviction policy module.
- Questions / unknowns: how expensive is salience computation at request time? offline vs online tradeoffs. Does clustering require extra metadata per token chunk (embedding)?
- Quick experiment idea: build a synthetic workload with conversation threads of length 8k tokens, compare full-KV vs top-k-sparse-KV hitrate and return perplexity on held-out continuation. Metric: quality delta per 1% memory saved.

Paper 2 — "PatchMatch Attention: Localized Key Matching for Long Contexts" (talk takeaways)
- Claim: restrict attention candidate keys via approximate nearest-neighbor hashing localized to sliding windows, then refine with small top-k.
- Engineering note: good fit for GPU kernels that want regular work; avoids O(n^2) but still captures far-field matches.
- For Redwood runtime: could be a compile-time kernel choice for certain model variants. Might be worth adding an option to the kernel selector flagged as "approx-attend-local".
- TODO: ask infra if adding a small L2-ANN service in front of serving path is acceptable latency-wise. Slack note to #infra: "latency budget for an ANN pre-step (50-150us) acceptable for 2-tier requests?"

Paper 3 — "Quantized KV and Far-Field Retrieval Stability" (notes)
- Finds that low-bit quantization of KV (4-bit) is more robust if you use per-chunk bias-correction and a small re-scaling during retrieval.
- Practical: saves memory on deduped KV stores for long-session user histories.
- Concern: quantization noise may interact poorly with attention sparsity heuristics — need joint ablation.

Synthesis / hypotheses I want to test quickly:
- H1: A top-k sparse KV eviction (size governed by model-token tradeoff) yields >20% memory reduction with <1.5% relative quality drop on multi-turn dialogue evals.
- H2: PatchMatch-style candidate pruning combined with re-ranking achieves similar quality to dense attention at 0.5-0.7x compute.
- H3: Quantized KV + small bias-correction reduces memory by 2-3x with moderate engineering cost and minimal runtime overhead if done at chunk granularity.

Experiment plan (minimal reproducible):
1) Dataset: internal convo-sim-sampled-1000 (threads with diverse recency/salience). Use 10 seeds.
2) Models: choose a mid-size open model we already have in catalog (v2-7b-quant and v2-13b-quant analog) — pick a cheap option for iteration.
3) Conditions: baseline (full KV), sparse-k (k=512,256,128), patchmatch-proxy, quant-kv (4-bit + bias-corr).
4) Metrics: generation ROC-like chart: quality (perp / chrF / ROUGE) vs memory and per-token latency percentile (50/95/99). Cost estimate per 1k tokens.
5) Quick infra notes: will need a small mod to our runtime to toggle KV eviction policy and to produce KV stats (kept_count, hit_rate, eviction_count) — open PR: rinf-kv-experiments#98.

Immediate next actions (short):
- [ ] Prototype an offline evaluator: adapt existing eval harness (evals/synthetic-run) to load sparse-k policies. (owner: me).
- [ ] Slack infra to ask about ANN pre-step latency budget and potential microservice cost (owner: Aisha).
- [ ] Draft an RFC skeleton for a "sparse-kv eviction" feature (one-pager outlining API, config, metrics) — aim to share with Jonas and Platform Eng next week.

Notes from workshop discussion (NeurIPS parallel session)
- People keep circling joint design: algorithm <-> kernel <-> routing stack. If one optimizes just the algorithm (paper), it rarely maps to kernel-friendly ops; you need a middle layer that turns algorithmic choices into batchable GPU-friendly ops. This matches Redwood's compilation + kernel selection layer sweet spot.
- A few teams mentioned "run-time profile-guided eviction" — basically log distribution of prefix lengths and use that to choose policy. Could be implemented as part of Console (Optimize suggestions).

Loose ideas for product hooks (if experiments look promising)
- Console suggestion: "Enable sparse-KV mode" with expected token cost savings estimate for last 30 days of trace.
- Dedicated customers: offer an "extended-context memory pack" (KV-backed, quantized) as an add-on for predictable pricing.

Random scratch mental notes (don't forget):
- Revisit RINF-1278 (eviction telemetry) to see existing telemetry keys.
- Keep experiment small to avoid blocking infra capacity quotas. Use local simulated GPUs initially.
- Link to paper pdfs + slides in the linked_artifacts list before moving to RFC.

Questions for collaborators:
- Aisha: can you prototype a tiny ANN pre-step in Go? How big is the latency/ops cost for 1M keys?
- Jonas: is there a simple console hook I can reuse for offering a toggle and showing estimated savings?

End of dump. Will clean up into an RFC outline once I have two runs' worth of numbers.
